title: The rejected stone (Matthew 21:33–46)
hookLine: cut, left out, passed over: the stone the builders threw away
tomorrow: everyone's invited off the street. so why is one guest thrown out?

cards: Cut from the team. Left off the invite. The name nobody picks.
This week, somewhere close, somebody is the one set aside. Jesus tells a story about a vineyard owner who rents his land to tenants and goes away.
At harvest he sends servants to collect his share, and the tenants beat them, kill them, stone them. Last, he sends his son: "They will reverence my son." They don't.
"This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance." And they do. Then Jesus asks what the owner will do, and quotes a psalm about a stone.

teach.b: Here is the stone: "The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?" Builders sort stones all day.
This one they looked at and tossed aside.
And it ends up at the corner, where two walls meet, the piece the rest of the building lines up with.

The words come from Psalm 118, a song from Israel's own worship. In Christian reading, the son and the stone are Jesus himself, rejected and then raised, and Peter's first letter takes up the same line.
Matthew is careful about who heard the story as aimed at them: "when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they perceived that he spake of them."

teach.h: LEADERS IN THAT ROOM, THAT DAY.
teach.b: Leaders in that room, that day, not a whole people. So what does this give a regular week? A way of looking.
The one everyone else has set aside may be the one the whole thing ends up lining up with. The psalm calls that turn the Lord's doing, and a marvel.

how: Some Christian hymns and prayers call Christ the cornerstone, from this psalm line, and Psalm 118 is also sung in Jewish worship as part of the Hallel psalms of praise.

games.q: you're house-sitting for a neighbor who's away for months. by now it feels like your place, and her rules feel optional. what does the tenants' story warn about?
o: forgetting whose house it actually is.
taking too much care of someone's things.
trusting a neighbor with your keys.
games.why: the tenants started treating the vineyard as theirs, and the owner's son as the obstacle. the story begins with forgetting whose it is.

practice: Take a pen and write the first name of one person who's been left out lately: at school, at work, in your family. Under it, write one thing they bring that nobody's noticing. Keep the paper somewhere you'll see it.
